title: 'Why Does He Need to Prove Himself?': Ashwin Rallies Behind Kohli Ahead of 2027 World Cup
excerpt: The retired spinner's defence of India's all-time leading ODI run-scorer underscores a deeper tension between meritocracy and legacy in Indian cricket.
body:
Virat Kohli has never been one to suffer doubters quietly. So when the former India captain told reporters this week that he does not "have to prove" his worth to anyone ahead of the 2027 ODI World Cup in South Africa, it was less a plea and more a warning: he intends to be there, and he is not interested in auditions.

The remarks, delivered with Kohli's characteristic directness, came amid a fresh round of speculation about whether India's senior players would — or should — feature in the tournament. Former captain Sourav Ganguly had publicly predicted that both Kohli and Rohit Sharma might skip the World Cup entirely, opting instead to focus on T20s and Tests. Sanjay Manjrekar, never far from a Kohli-related hot take, suggested the batter was "sensitive to criticism" and needed to demonstrate his form in bilateral series before claiming a squad berth.

**Ashwin weighs in**

Enter R. Ashwin, Kohli's former teammate and a man whose analytical mind extends well beyond off-spin variations. Backing Kohli publicly, Ashwin argued that a player with 14,797 ODI runs, 50 centuries, and a batting average above 57 had long since settled any questions about his credentials. "Why does a man with that record need to prove himself?" Ashwin asked on his YouTube channel, adding that the constant cycle of senior players being asked to justify their existence was "exhausting and unnecessary."

https://www.instagram.com/p/virat.kohli

The intervention matters. Ashwin, who retired from international cricket in December 2024 during the Brisbane Test, carries moral authority precisely because he is no longer competing for a spot himself. His defence of Kohli is not self-serving; it is a commentary on a cricketing culture that treats every lean patch as a referendum on a career.

**The form question**

None of this means Kohli is beyond scrutiny. His Test retirement in early 2025, following a difficult Australia tour, raised legitimate questions about his appetite for the longest format. In the IPL, where he continues to turn out for Royal Challengers Bengaluru, his performances have been solid rather than spectacular this season — valuable runs in a title-contending side, but not the match-defining innings that once made him the league's signature player.

The 2027 World Cup, however, is ODI cricket — the format in which Kohli's record is most formidable. India's selectors, led by Ajit Agarkar, face a delicate balancing act: manage the transition to a younger core while retaining players whose big-tournament experience is irreplaceable. Kohli, at 37 by the time the World Cup begins, would be playing in what is almost certainly his last global tournament.

**The diaspora divided**

Among NRI fans, the Kohli debate has split along familiar lines. On X (formerly Twitter) and in WhatsApp groups from New Jersey to Melbourne, some argue that sentiment should never override form; others insist that Kohli's six-tournament experience — including the 2023 World Cup, where he was Player of the Tournament despite India's final heartbreak — makes him an automatic pick. The debate mirrors a broader tension in Indian cricket fandom abroad: the desire for a ruthless, performance-based meritocracy versus the deep emotional attachment to players who have defined an era.

**What to watch**

India's ODI calendar in the second half of 2026 will provide the data points that matter. A home series against England and a tour of Sri Lanka are pencilled in, and Kohli's performances there will either vindicate his stance or hand ammunition to his critics. For now, Ashwin's backing has shifted the narrative — from "can Kohli still do it?" to "why are we still asking?"
